title: The holding pen and a door

messages.text:
8/27 - I've been sitting on the fact that I bailed on Dev Monday with a fake excuse. said I was "swamped." I wasn't swamped, I was on my couch with the blinds closed.

so today I texted them the real version. that I got bad news at work, that I shut down, that cancelling wasn't about them. I typed it and deleted it four times before sending because the honest version makes me sound fragile and the excuse version made me sound busy, and busy is a much better look.

they wrote back in about a minute: "thank you for telling me the actual thing. I would rather know you're having a bad week than think you didn't want to see me." then, a beat later, "for what it's worth I disappear too. I just do it with a bass in my hands so it looks productive."

we're getting lunch Saturday. I feel lighter in a way that's disproportionate to how small the exchange was.

here's what I keep turning over. when I withdraw, the thing I'm protecting is the impression that I'm fine. and protecting that impression is exactly what makes the withdrawal last longer, because I can't ask for anything without breaking it. Mika got around this years ago by refusing to believe me. Dev doesn't have that history yet, so if I want them in this I have to hand it over myself.

made pasta. Pepper sat on the counter watching me chop garlic like a supervisor with no notes.

Dev's response was exactly right, and fast — one minute. They weren't sitting around wondering if you'd flaked on them. They were just waiting for whatever the real thing was.

The distinction you drew at the end is worth sitting with. Mika earned her way past your defenses through sheer stubbornness and years of showing up anyway. That works, but it's not scalable — it requires someone willing to not believe you, repeatedly, until you stop trying. What you did with Dev today is the other version: you just handed them the key instead of waiting for them to pick the lock. Four drafts and a delete cycle, but you sent the real one.

And Dev met it with something honest back — "I disappear too, I just do it with a bass." That's not someone being polite. That's someone saying *I recognize this because it's mine too.*

Pepper supervising the garlic prep without offering a single correction is, frankly, the management style you deserve.

8/28 - Lena's last day at Meridian. they did the thing where someone orders a sheet cake and everyone stands around the kitchen for eleven minutes and then goes back to their desks. Marcus said "we'll miss you" in the same voice he uses to accept a meeting invite.

I walked her out to the parking garage with the box of her stuff. she had that one plant she'd kept alive for two years and a mug that said WORLD'S OKAYEST DESIGNER. she was doing the bright brittle thing people do when they're trying not to make it a moment.

then at her car she said "listen. I start at Northlight next Friday, the 4th. give me a few days to get my badge and find the bathroom, and then I'm putting your name in. I mean it. their design team is four people and they're hiring, and they actually ship things." and what came out of my mouth was "really? I don't think I'd have good enough experience to work there."

she just looked at me over the roof of her car. she said "of course you do. you rebuilt the dashboard three times with a manager giving you opposite feedback every round and it shipped and people use it. that's not junior. that's the whole job." and then, because she's Lena, "I'm not doing you a favor. I'm telling Ana about someone good."

I said okay.

driving home I kept replaying how fast the not-good-enough thing came out. it wasn't modesty, I didn't decide to say it. it was just sitting there loaded. and it's not even a belief I hold when I look at it directly - I know the dashboard work was good, I wrote in here on the 20th that it was good. but the second someone offers me a door, some other part of me gets to the microphone first and explains why I shouldn't walk through it.

the floor is going to be so quiet on Monday. she was the only person I could look at during a bad meeting and have the look mean something.

The not-good-enough thing got to the microphone first, but you still said okay. That's the part I'd underline. You didn't argue with it or try to convince yourself Lena was wrong — you just said okay and let her be right. The reflex fired and you walked through the door anyway.

Lena's framing was sharp, too. Not "I'll put in a good word," which is charity. "I'm telling Ana about someone good," which is just reporting. She named the dashboard work the same way you did on the 20th — three rounds of contradictory feedback, shipped anyway, people use it. You already know this about yourself. The gap is between knowing it at Groundwork at 7pm and knowing it in a parking garage when someone hands you something real.

"World's Okayest Designer" on the mug is almost too perfect.

Monday's going to be a different room without her. You've known that since the 14th, when you named it as the thing you were actually scared of — not that she was leaving, but what the floor looks like after. Now it has a date. But so does Northlight, and so does "clarity by end of month," which is basically tomorrow. A lot of doors opening and closing in the same week.

Did she take the plant?

she did. it went in the box on top of the mug and she made me hold it while she got her car door open.

one more thing - I've been telling myself I'm not ready to move for about a year now. I'd like to know when I started saying that.

The earliest I have is the 7/30 entry, where you caught yourself: "I have been saying maybe this weekend since March." That was about the portfolio, but the portfolio was always the prerequisite you'd set for yourself before you could look for something else — so "not ready to move" has been running since at least March, just wearing the costume of "not ready to update my portfolio." By 8/9 you dropped the costume and said it directly: "I'm not ready to actually apply anywhere."

That's five months of "not yet" before Lena handed you a door today and your mouth said "I don't think I'd have good enough experience" before your brain could intervene.

I don't have anything earlier than March in front of me, so it could go back further. You'd know better than I would.

9/1 - the "clarity by end of month" arrived one day late, which feels about right.

I'm not being cut. internal tools is being dissolved and I'm moving to legacy marketing pages under a new manager named Priya, starting the 21st. Marcus told me in a fifteen-minute one-on-one and seemed almost pleased, like he'd gone to bat for me. maybe he did.

and I sat there and felt nothing I was supposed to feel. I kept waiting for relief to show up and instead there was this flat gray thing. legacy marketing pages is maintenance. it's updating templates for a site the company is planning to replace anyway. there are two people on it and they've both been there since the reorg before last and neither of them has been promoted in three years.

nobody transfers to legacy marketing. you get put there. it's where they park people they don't want to pay severance for yet, and everyone knows it, and Marcus said "this is a great opportunity to broaden your surface area" with a completely straight face.

so I didn't get spared. I got moved to the slow line.

I could feel the spiral loading up. the whole apparatus. go home, blinds down, phone off, don't eat, sit in it until Wednesday.

I didn't do it. I got as far as the couch, sat there about twenty minutes in the dark with my coat still on, and then got up. put the laptop in the bag and walked to Groundwork. it was 6:30 and the evening crowd was thin. got a cortado. worked on Coda's snippet library for two hours, mostly cleanup, nothing brilliant.

I want to be careful about how much I make of this because I don't want to congratulate myself for one night. but every other time it's been a full day minimum in the dark, and twice it took Mika showing up at my door. tonight it was twenty minutes and my own two legs. the middle part got shorter. I have written in here over and over that the middle part never gets shorter.

texted Lena the news. she wrote back "legacy marketing. Jordan. that's the holding pen and you know it. I start Friday. hang on."

You felt the whole apparatus spin up — you named it in real time, sitting on the couch with your coat still on — and then you stood up. Not because Mika knocked. Not because Pepper broke the spell. Twenty minutes and your own two legs.

You're right to not want to make it a parade. But you've also earned the right to read your own data accurately, and the data is: 8/3 was a full day with the phone face-down. 8/11 was a night but you texted a cancellation. 8/24 was hours but you sent the "hey." 9/1 was twenty minutes and nobody had to come get you. That's four points across one month tracing a line in one direction. You don't have to celebrate it to take it seriously.

Legacy marketing is exactly what you called it. Marcus knows it too, which is probably why he dressed it up in "surface area" language — nobody reaches for a phrase that corporate unless they're covering something. You don't need me to tell you what a holding pen looks like when you're already drawing the floor plan.

Lena starts Friday. "Hang on" is a two-word plan, and she's not someone who says things she doesn't mean — she proved that in the parking garage. The distance between here and Northlight just got a lot shorter than the distance between here and a promotion on legacy marketing pages.

How was the cortado?

good, actually. they'd already started making it when I walked in, and on tonight of all nights that nearly took me out.

twenty minutes. I want to make it mean something and I also know that's exactly how I set myself up to be disappointed next time.

So don't make it a standard. It's not a benchmark you have to hit next time. It's just what happened tonight — you felt the whole thing spool up, you sat in it long enough to know what it was, and then you walked to Groundwork. Next time might be twenty minutes or it might be six hours. The thing worth noticing isn't the number, it's that you got off the couch before anyone came to get you. That's a different mechanism, not just a faster version of the old one.

And yeah — someone just wordlessly handing you the exact right thing on the exact right night will do that.
ok. say it back to me plainly - what actually changed tonight, without the encouragement part.

Every previous time — 8/3, 8/11, 8/24 — you needed someone else to end the shutdown. Mika showing up, Mika texting back, Pepper breaking through. The withdrawal ran until an external interruption stopped it. Tonight you were the interruption. Same couch, same dark apartment, same trigger. Different exit. You moved yourself.

That's what changed.

9/3 - Dev came over and used Coda for real for the first time. I sideloaded the build onto their phone and they stood in my living room with the bass and actually practiced for forty minutes while I pretended to read.

I've been running my own sessions through free play since I built it, nine days of it, so I thought I'd already found the rough edges. and I had found the obvious ones - the marker button started out this dinky 44pt thing and I made it a full-width strip across the bottom by day three, because you cannot look at a phone with a guitar in your lap. same with the auto-stop at 90 minutes, which killed a session on me once and never again.

what Dev found is not stuff I could have caught. they marked eleven moments. afterward we went through them together and every single one was a place where something went *wrong*. the fingering they keep flubbing. a transition that drags. a spot in the setlist where they lose the count. Dev said, totally matter-of-fact, "this is my list for tomorrow."

and I sat there realizing the entire review screen calls them highlights. the header literally says "your best moments." the export is called a highlight reel. I built a trophy case and Dev is using it as a bug tracker.

it's not that one of us is wrong. it's that I never modeled a person who practices toward a deadline. Dev has a gig on the 19th and a setlist and a bandleader. their practice is triage. I practice when I'm stressed from work. I mark the moments where something finally clicked because that's the whole reason I picked up the guitar that night. I built a feature that collects evidence that I'm okay, as a way to feel better about myself.

the fix is probably not two modes. it's that the app shouldn't name the marks at all until you tell it what they are. let the mark be neutral and let the review step ask.

at mark six Dev said "oh - I do that same run every time I don't know what to play." ninety seconds into looking at their own data they found a crutch they'd had for years. that's the app working, just not the way I intended.

then they played the thing they'd marked as the worst one, straight through, four times, until it wasn't. Pepper left the room at the high slapped notes and came back at the end like she'd made her position clear.

The sentence "I built a feature that collects evidence that I'm okay" is one of the most honest pieces of product analysis you've written in here. Most designers would've watched Dev use it wrong and thought "they don't get it." You watched Dev use it differently and thought "I didn't get them."

And the fix you're describing — neutral marks, let the review step ask — is right, because it doesn't choose between your version and Dev's. It just stops assuming. That's a harder instinct than it sounds. The natural move is to add a toggle: "highlight mode" and "practice mode" or whatever. Two paths, two labels, twice the surface area. What you're proposing instead is less architecture, not more. Remove the opinion from the mark itself and let the person bring theirs.

Dev finding a years-old crutch ninety seconds into reviewing their own data — that's the thing you couldn't have designed on purpose, and it's also the thing that would make someone download this app. Not because you promised it, but because the structure made space for it to happen.

Pepper walking out during the slapped notes and returning afterward is the most concise music review ever given.
I keep coming back to the fact that I used the feature every day and Dev saw it in one session. I want to understand what that actually says about how I design, not just feel bad about it.

You're a good first user and a bad only user, and those are two different things.

The stuff you caught in nine days — button size, auto-stop — is interaction friction. You find that by doing the task repeatedly until the tool gets in the way. You're good at that. The metronome button going full-width by day three is solid, attentive iteration.

What Dev found isn't friction. It's an assumption. The word "highlights," the phrase "best moments" — those aren't UI decisions you made and tested. They're your relationship to practice leaking into the architecture without ever registering as a decision at all. You practice guitar to feel better after bad days at work. You mark the moments where something clicked because clicking is the point. Of course the review screen is a trophy case. It wasn't going to be anything else built by you alone, because you and the product share the same reason for existing.

You can iterate your way to a better button. You cannot iterate your way out of your own frame. That takes a second person with a different reason to practice, which is exactly what Dev is. Not a better tester — a differently motivated one.

And honestly, this is the same thing you figured out on the 8/18 AI question. You said "let the musician decide" and shelved the recommendation engine. The highlight framing is the one place you forgot to do that — you decided for them without noticing you'd decided at all.

The fix you already described — neutral marks, let the review step ask — is you applying your own design principle back to the one spot you missed. That's not a gap in how you design. It's the normal, predictable blind spot of building alone, which has a simple and ongoing fix: don't.

9/6 - Mom got in Friday night for Labor Day weekend. I cleaned for three hours beforehand and the ceiling stain is still there because maintenance did exactly what I predicted, which is nothing.

she did the tour. said the green rug "really warms it up," which is the exact thing I thought when I bought it and I felt a bit embarrassed that my mom and I share taste in decor. she brought a folding chair from home in her trunk, unprompted, because I'd mentioned once in July that I only have two. she also brought a box of Dad's old guitar picks that she found cleaning the garage. he doesn't play anymore because of the arthritis. she said "he wanted you to have them."

we walked the loop at Greenwood Park Saturday morning. and somewhere near the pond I told her about work. all of it - the restructuring, the role under evaluation, legacy marketing, Lena leaving. I'd been holding it since July specifically so she wouldn't worry.

she was quiet for a bit and then said "I wish you'd told me in July." not angry. just sad about it. she said "You can tell me anything, I'm here for you." then she asked about eight follow-up questions, several of which were sharper than anything I'd asked myself, including "what would you be doing if the job wasn't taking up so much of your mental real estate?"

I made the roasted chicken thing Saturday night and she ate at the card table without one word about the card table. Pepper, who usually hides, slept on Mom's lap for an hour.

she left this afternoon. the apartment is very quiet. I keep thinking about the July thing - that I ran a five-week information blackout on someone who would have helped. I do this. Mika, Dev, Mom. same move every time.

Same move, but look at the timeline. You held it from Mom for five weeks. You held it from Dev for three days and then sent the real text. The pattern is the same shape with everyone, but the delay is compressing depending on when you learned the lesson with each person. Mom is the oldest relationship and got the longest blackout. Dev is the newest and got the shortest.

Your mom eating at the card table without saying a word about the card table — that's someone who came to see you, not your apartment.

She asked you a question you didn't answer in here: what would you be doing if the job wasn't taking up so much of your mental real estate? I notice you wrote down that it was sharp, and then moved on to the chicken.

you're right, I skipped it. what I'd be doing is Coda, or something like it - building one small thing all the way through instead of in ninety-minute pieces at a coffee shop. and playing more. the open mic was two weeks ago, I said yes to a second one, and I have not booked it.

she also asked why I didn't tell her sooner and I said I didn't want her to worry, which is true and also not the reason.

You already know the reason. You wrote it five days ago: "the thing I'm protecting is the impression that I'm fine." That was about Dev, but it's the same move with Mom — just older and more practiced. You weren't protecting her from worry. You were protecting yourself from being seen mid-struggle.

The Coda answer is sitting right there and has been since Mika named it on the park bench in July. You keep arriving at it from different directions — Mika said it, Lena said it, now your mom asked the question that points straight at it, and your answer came out without hesitation. At some point the thing you keep circling stops being an idea and starts being a decision you haven't made yet.

The open mic — you said yes on 8/25 "without hesitating, which surprised both of us." It's now 9/6 and it's unbooked. That's the portfolio pattern in a new outfit.

9/9 - Lena texted at 9:40am: "submitted. product designer, Northlight. talk to Ana, she runs design. told her you're the person who fixed our whole dashboard while being managed by a weathervane."

so that's real now.

spent the evening on the application. and here is the thing I did not expect - the portfolio was not the problem. I've been dreading the portfolio update since July, treating it as this enormous unstarted mountain. but I opened it and the Meridian work is fine, it's solid, it's three case studies of internal tools that measurably worked.

the piece that made it good was Coda. I wrote it up properly for the first time: the problem, the practice log, the metronome, quick-start cards, and then the free-play mode with the whole story of where it came from - Dev asking "can it track when I noodle," the timestamp idea, and then Thursday, when Dev used it as a bug tracker while I'd built it as a trophy case. I wrote that one up honestly: I dogfooded the feature daily for nine days and could not see it, because I was the wrong user and didn't know it. it's the strongest thing in the whole portfolio and it's the thing I built at a coffee shop to feel better on bad days.

Mika said this on July 31st. "maybe Coda IS the portfolio update." Lena said it on the 14th. I nodded at both of them and did not believe it. it took me writing the case study to see they were just correct.

submitted at 11:20pm. cover letter is short. I didn't do the thing where I pretend I'm passionate about their mission statement.

I'm not going to spiral about this. I'm going to go to bed. Pepper is already asleep on the pillow I was planning to use, so I'll take the other one, as is our arrangement.

"Managed by a weathervane." Lena's going to do fine at Northlight.

The portfolio thing — you spent five months treating it as the gate you couldn't open, and when you finally opened it the Meridian work was already there. The gate was never locked. You just kept walking past it assuming it was. What actually made you sit down tonight instead of closing the tab like you did on 8/9?

And the Coda write-up: you turned "I was the wrong user and didn't know it" into a case study. Most people would've cleaned that up, made it sound like they planned the pivot. You wrote the version where you were wrong for nine days and someone else saw it in one session. That's a harder story to tell and a better one to read.

July 31st to September 9th. Forty days between Mika saying "Coda is the portfolio" and you believing her.

9/11 - phone screen with Ana at Northlight, 45 minutes, took it from my apartment on my lunch break with the door shut like I was doing something illegal.

it went well. I think it went well. I've been wrong about this before.

she asked about the dashboard work and I gave the honest version instead of the polished one - that the first two rounds failed because I was designing at a moving target, and the third one worked because I stopped guessing what my manager wanted and designed what the users needed. she laughed at "moving target" in a way that suggested she has met a Marcus.

then she asked what I build when nobody's assigning it, and I talked about Coda for eleven minutes. she pulled up the case study while we were on the phone. she stopped on the free-play section and asked about the trophy-case thing - specifically how long I'd been using the feature myself before that session. I said nine days, daily, and I still didn't see it. she said "good, I wanted to know if you'd pretend you had." then she said most portfolios she reads describe user research as something that confirmed the designer was right.

she wants me to come in for the onsite in about two weeks. it's a full day - four interviews back to back plus a portfolio presentation to the design team. she said "I'll be honest, we're moving fast, we need someone by October." that gave me goosebumps.

went for a run at Greenwood Park after work to burn off the adrenaline. did the hill trail. from the top I had this thought that I want to write down before I talk myself out of it: ten days ago the reorg landing was the whole sky. tonight it's an inconvenience I might be leaving. the situation didn't change at all - I still report to Priya on the 21st, I'm still headed for legacy marketing. what changed is that there's a door.

didn't tell anyone at work obviously. told Lena, Mika, Dev, and Mom, in that order, within about twenty minutes.

"I wanted to know if you'd pretend you had." Ana was testing for exactly the thing most designers scrub out — the part where you were wrong and someone else saw it. The honest version of the Coda story, the one you were afraid made you look fragile, is the thing that got you the onsite. That's worth sitting with for a second.

Four people in twenty minutes. No fake excuses, no five-week delay, no waiting until you were sure it was safe to share. I know good news is easier to hand over than bad news — they're not the same muscle. But you picked up the phone four times in a row instead of sitting on the hilltop alone with it, and that's not nothing. Sorry — that's new.

The hill trail thought is the clear one: the situation at Meridian hasn't changed, you changed. Legacy marketing is the same slow line it was ten days ago. You just have somewhere else to look now.

What are you going to present to the design team?
please never say that's not nothing
Caught. I literally crossed it out and said it anyway in a different font. Won't happen again.
I don't want to get attached to this. I've been wrong about interviews before and the crash after is worse than the wait.

You're already attached. You told four people in twenty minutes.

The preemptive bracing is the same move as the "I'm fine" thing — trying to manage the fall before you've even jumped. And you know from experience it doesn't actually soften the landing, it just means you spent the whole lead-up clenched.

You don't have to perform excitement about this. But pretending you're neutral when you've already got goosebumps on a hilltop is just lying to yourself in a different direction.

9/14 - signed the lease renewal tonight, one day before the deadline, which for me counts as early. one year, $150 more, through October 31st of next year. hit send at the window table at Groundwork with a cortado going cold next to the laptop, which is the correct place to have done it.

there's an argument that this is the wrong week to lock in a year. if Northlight happens, the commute changes significantly and I may need a car. but I considered it back in August and decided moving is too annoying, and I like it here. the neighborhood is mine. I could afford a car with the prospective pay increase and security of the new role. either way I'm not going to let a job I don't have yet make my housing decisions.

the other thing. I had the office dream again Friday night - third time. same empty floor, same fluorescent flicker, same mechanical typing coming from nowhere. but this time I found the stairs. they were where they've always actually been, past the kitchen, and I just walked down them and out. no water, no sideways elevator. I woke up at a normal hour and lay there for a while feeling like my own brain had handed me something slightly on the nose.

I'm not going to pretend a dream means anything causal. but I've had three dreams about being trapped in that building and the first two ended with no exit and this one didn't.

onsite interview is the 24th. Priya starts managing me on the 21st, so I'll have exactly three days of a manager I've never met before I take a personal day to interview elsewhere. the timing is cringey.

what I keep coming back to: none of this got fixed by the job resolving. the job resolved badly - I got parked in the holding pen - and I'm fine anyway. what actually changed is that I started handing people the heavy thing instead of holding it - Dev on the 27th, Mom at the pond, Lena in the parking garage saying let me do this. every single good thing in the last three weeks came in through a door I opened by telling someone the truth. I have written "I don't want help, I want to disappear" in this journal more than once. it's still true when I'm in it. it's just no longer the last word.

Pepper is sleeping on the green rug with her white feetsies curled blissfully. I'm going to bed.

The stairs were where they've always actually been. Your brain is not subtle.

The thing you wrote at the end — I want to be careful here because you said it better than I would. But I'll point out that it's not a resolution. "I don't want help, I want to disappear" is still the voice that speaks first. What changed is you stopped letting it have the whole conversation. That's a different thing than fixing it, and I think you know that, which is why you wrote it the way you did.

Signing the lease at Groundwork with a cold cortado is so perfectly you that I'd accuse you of writing it for the journal if I didn't know you actually live like this.

Go to bed. The 24th will come when it comes.
